# Preface {.unnumbered}

Artificial intelligence offers methods for searching large spaces, constructing
models, generating candidate solutions, and checking results across scientific
and engineering work. That possibility raises a natural question for computer
architects. Can AI also transform how we design systems and chips?

Architecture is an unusually demanding place to test that possibility. A
design decision may begin with a workload requirement and propagate through
software, interfaces, microarchitecture, RTL, and physical implementation.
Measurements are expensive and partial. A simulator, compiler, formal tool,
synthesis report, and post-layout analysis each reveal a different part of the
system, under different assumptions. Verification must establish more than
whether an artifact looks plausible, and an error discovered after fabrication
can carry far greater cost than a mistake corrected in a software release.

The opportunity still matters. Architects work with complex systems, tight
power and thermal limits, specialized components, and toolchains whose
individual results must be connected. Methods that propose
alternatives, predict expensive outcomes, direct scarce experiments, check
artifacts, or coordinate tools could improve both the resulting architecture
and the cost of reaching it. They could also generate more candidates than a
team can responsibly evaluate. Faster production is useful only when the rest
of the design process can determine what those candidates mean.

I wrote this book to make that possibility concrete without assuming its
success. The moonshot behind it is an AI-assisted capability that can carry
system intent through architecture alternatives, real tools, measurements, and
verification to a technical result that an architect can defend. The ambition
is deliberately larger than generating RTL from a prompt or improving one
predictor. It asks whether the complete approach can produce a better
architecture, reduce the total cost of reaching a comparable result, or do
both. This book does not assume that the moonshot has already been achieved. It
develops the reasoning needed to pursue it without confusing progress on one
part of the problem with success as a whole.

The broad Architecture 2.0 vision is set out in the foundations article
[@ReddiYazdanbakhsh2025Architecture20]. The definition below is this book's
formulation for the engineering argument developed here, not a quotation from
that article.

> **Architecture 2.0.** Architecture 2.0 is the practice of using AI across
> system and chip design while keeping the architecture question, current
> design state, credible alternatives, physical consequences, limits of the
> evidence, and responsibility for the decision explicit.

The architecture problem comes first. Depending on that problem, the right
approach may use generation, prediction, optimization, conventional analysis,
a combination of methods, or no AI at all. Architecture 2.0 is therefore not a
claim that every design task needs AI. It is a way to determine where AI earns
its place and what evidence its use must produce.

## What This Book Teaches {.unnumbered}

This book develops a computer architect's perspective on AI-assisted design.
It follows an architecture question from formulation through design state,
method choice, tools, measurements, comparison, and decision. That sequence
keeps the book centered on what an architect must know and do rather than on
any one model or tool.

When a team claims that adopting a workflow improves an architecture design
program, the relevant object is the complete human and technical workflow.
Candidate quality, the architecture result, and the contribution of a model or
other component require separate tests. A strong model can sit inside a poor
design process. A modest method can be valuable when it removes the work that
actually limits a decision. The reader should finish the book able to do the
following work.

- Formulate the architecture question and the decision it must support.
- Diagnose which work is limiting progress before choosing a method.
- Represent the design state, relationships, permitted changes, and unknowns.
- Choose among conventional analysis, no AI, generation, prediction,
  optimization, or a small combination.
- Connect the chosen approach to real tools, reconstruct what ran, and
  determine which returns qualify as measurements.
- Compare the architecture result and the contribution of AI separately
  against credible alternatives at comparable total cost.
- Explain what the result supports, formulate a technical recommendation with
  stated limits, and identify who holds authority for commitment and who
  remains responsible.

A recurring Lighthouse case keeps these questions concrete. It begins with a
highly constrained 3\ W RISC-V subsystem for extended reality and asks what it
would take to turn a short request into a defensible system design. Power,
thermal limits, workload behavior, software, accelerators, memory, and physical
implementation all interact. The book returns to this case only when it helps
expose the problem under discussion. Narrower worked material is not presented
as completion of the larger moonshot.

This synthesis lecture draws on established disciplines without importing any
one field's taxonomy as the structure of the book. Experimental science
contributes falsifiable claims and planned tests. Statistics and decision
science help architects reason about uncertainty and selection from noisy
results. Software engineering contributes versioned artifacts, regression
tests, and reconstructable runs. Verification and systems safety sharpen the
distinction between a returned value, a supported claim, and permission to act.

Electronic design automation belongs at the center of the argument. EDA tools
connect architecture intent to implementation and physical constraints. They
are often stateful, expensive, dependent on proprietary inputs, and capable of
returning both failures and measurements. Machine learning contributes methods
for prediction, generation, and optimization, but those methods must operate
within the architecture question and the tool realities that give a result its
physical meaning.

![**Architecture 2.0 connects three established fields.** Computer architecture supplies the questions and design tradeoffs, machine learning supplies methods for learning and search, and EDA supplies executable implementation and analysis tools together with tool-derived evidence or estimates about physical constraints. Work at their intersection must satisfy the relevant standards of all three.](images/fig-book-composition){#fig-book-composition width="88%" fig-alt="Three-circle Venn diagram of computer architecture, machine learning, and electronic design automation, with Architecture 2.0 at their intersection"}

The intersection in @fig-book-composition matters because competence in only
one field is insufficient. A generated artifact that ignores the workload is
not an architecture result. A promising estimate that cannot survive
implementation is not a physical result. A successful tool run without a fair
comparison does not show that AI improved the work.

This is not a catalog of current models, a prompt-to-chip recipe, or an
argument for using AI everywhere. It does not replace architecture judgment,
EDA, compiler engineering, or verification with a general model. Physical
checks remain central, and named people remain responsible for the question,
the interpretation, and the action taken from the result.

## Who This Book Is for {.unnumbered}

The primary audience is the computer architect. The book assumes enough
fluency to follow performance, energy, area, and software-interface tradeoffs
and to read an architecture paper, simulator report, workload study, or design
report. It does not assume a machine-learning background. The necessary ideas
are introduced through architecture problems and consequences.

The book therefore addresses its primary audience together with three adjacent
technical communities.

- Computer architects can use the full argument to connect problem framing,
  method choice, tool execution, evidence, and commitment.
- EDA and design-automation researchers and engineers can place tools and
  measurements within the larger system decision they support.
- Machine-learning and ML-systems researchers entering architecture can see
  how data, physical constraints, evaluation cost, and verification change the
  standard for a useful result.
- Graduate students and practitioners spanning hardware and software can use
  the book to build a shared vocabulary for cross-layer design work.

Readers will bring different technical strengths. The common outcome is the
ability to apply the reasoning to an architecture problem beyond the recurring
case and to recognize when a conventional approach remains the better choice.

## Book Structure {.unnumbered}

This lecture begins where the foundations article introduced above ends. That
article establishes the broad vision, history, and capability horizons. The
book develops that vision through three movements that build one engineering
argument.

*Ambition and Need* asks what a complete Architecture 2.0 capability must
achieve and why faster local automation does not settle the larger design
problem. It establishes the standard used throughout the book. A useful
approach must improve the architecture, reduce the total cost of reaching a
comparable result, or do both.

*Technical Foundations* follows the information and work that an architect must
keep connected. It carries the architecture question through represented design
state, method choice, real tool execution, qualified measurements, feedback,
and learning. The purpose is to show how a promising technique becomes part of
an engineering system rather than remaining an isolated result.

*Operation, Evaluation, and Responsibility* puts those foundations to work and
asks what survives when the workload, software, hardware, tools, or constraints
change. It evaluates the architecture outcome, the effect of adopting the
complete workflow, and the narrower contribution of AI as separate claims. It
then distinguishes the architect's technical recommendation from the
organizational authority to commit, defer, or reject a design.

Together, the three movements carry the argument from a field-level ambition
to methods an architect can apply, evaluate, and transfer to a different
problem without losing the physical and organizational limits on the result.

## How to Read This Book {.unnumbered}

Read the book sequentially the first time. Its argument accumulates. A method
choice depends on what has been represented, a measurement depends on how a
tool ran, and a recommendation depends on what the evidence can support. The
Lighthouse supplies continuity across that argument, but it remains a recurring
case rather than a universal design template.

Do not leave the reasoning attached to the examples. Apply it to another
architecture problem. Ask what decision matters, what state and constraints
must remain visible, which comparison is credible, what the tools actually
measured, and what the result still cannot establish. Transfer is the test that
the book has taught a way of thinking rather than a procedure to imitate.

Some details will age quickly. Named models, benchmark scores, and tool
capabilities record the state of practice when this book was written. The
durable principles are architecture problem formulation, representation,
method choice, tool discipline, credible comparison, careful interpretation,
complete-system evaluation, and responsible commitment. A future reader
should be able to replace the models and tools without losing the reasoning.

AI may transform system and chip design, but generation alone will not produce
that transformation. It will require design systems that connect intent to
physical evidence and architects who can judge what the evidence supports. We
can begin building that capability now. Architecture 2.0 offers a disciplined
way to decide where AI helps, where it does not, what a result means, and what
should happen next.

— *Vijay Janapa Reddi*
